author: C.J. GEOTIS
title: The moral of the story: Never give up - NewsBreak
text:
By C.J. GEOTIS ,
5 hours ago
Eight o’clock in the morning. We pushed Dan’s boat from the dock into Vaca Cut. This was one of those fabulous Florida Keys mornings when blood runs hot through the veins of offshore anglers. We already knew that, because the three of us had been rushing around looking for things we forgot to bring or promised to bring. I think it’s a mortal sin to promise to bring something we would need on this trip. Fortunately, there was no reason to keel-haul one or two of us for breaking this commandment.
Dan’s 900-hp, 36-foot Invincible jumped up on plane outside the short no-wake zone. We headed to a waypoint we use for catching yellowtail snappers, which I call YTs. The Atlantic Ocean was dead flat. There was a cool front settled in all around the Keys. We loved it. I had packed a red-white-and-blue hooded sweat jacket. I didn’t need it. At 45 mph it was a short run to the reef. The vibrant-blue sky was cloudless; I snapped a photo.
Now it was time to get to work. Dan, his friend Tim and I have fished together a number of times. It worked out great because we have become accustomed to each other and we quickly had an anchor holding the boat in place in around 60 feet of water. The first block of chum was bagged and chips and scraps of chum melted into perfect-sized pieces of chum.
Sadly, there was no current. Our beautiful chum floated in place directly behind the boat. We all groaned. “It’ll come around sooner or later,” I said, making the most optimistic face I could muster up.
A huge yellow jack swam in and out of our vision. Instantly, I made catching this fish my goal in life right then and there. Dan decided to drop a bait to the bottom. Tim cut small pieces of cut ballyhoos and drifted them on small hooks. Even though the current had been running very slowly, we all did what we wanted to do and decided to make the best of it.
Ya gotta love fisherpersons. We “manned” up and played the cards we were dealt. We worked without a sound for a while. Tim caught the first fish. It was a small fish but larger than the minimum size. It’s always nice to cover the first fish caught under the already prepared icy cold slurry of saltwater. We high-fived and celebrated, then got back to fishing.
Tim caught another yellowtail and put him under the ice. “It looked like the current had picked up just a bit,” Tim said.
I told him, "The first angler to catch a yellowtail that’s big enough to make the drag screech on his reel gets an award.” I guess I should have paid more attention to the fishing and not teasing Tim. “Fish on,” Tim yelled, as his drag screeched and groaned. It was a valiant fish fight. Tim was the ultimate winner. Dan netted the fish and we all marveled to see and measure an 18-inch yellowtail. What a beautiful fish. It was Tim’s biggest YT ever.
We fished for a while. I almost caught the big yellow jack I’d been chasing. Dan almost caught a big fish off the bottom and Tim, smiling, just did not care about anything. So, we rinsed the boat, cleaned up any debris or rubbish and prepared to do some mahi mahi trolling.
With outriggers in their working positions and ready for battle, we headed out for deeper water and bigger fish. It was still one of the best days of the year weather wise. We usually run four to six rods in different locations and rigged with different lures or baits. We also customarily mix plastic and artificial lures as well as chain rigged ballyhoos. We found ourselves in the middle of a gigantic area of scattered bay grass and Sargassum weed. We were surprised there were so few boats near us or almost at the horizon. We worked the area with Dan at the helm and in the tower. He was able to maneuver through the mess of weeds from the tower.
We moved quickly moving from several regular trolling spots and were not having any luck. It was time to “think out of the box” as the business expression goes. We cleared all the lines, brought the boat up on plane and roared to an area we had not fished for a long time. We moved possibly 10 miles. The water had less weeds floating in it, which we smiled about. We found big, solid patches of Sargassum and concentrated on watching for birds or debris.
Finally, a lone frigatebird came into sight. Dan did a great job of catching up to the big bird while Tim and I cut bait into to medium-size pieces that we would cast to visible mahi-mahis. It was getting to be afternoon and almost time to head home. We had traveled a long way, but with the introduction of the big frigatebird giving us indications of feeding fish beneath him. Our idea to move “out of the box” worked. The frigatebird moved away but we trolled the area where he had been. Dan made a close pass at one of the larger and thicker pads of weeds.
Two outriggers popped and line started running from reels. “This is it!” Dan shouted. "All hands-on deck! Battle stations.” A big school of mahi-mahis surrounded the boat. We boated the first two while Tim caught another. We just kept casting and catching until we had our fill and the school swam away. Bottom line: six quality mahi-mahis covered in ice.
The moral of the story is, NEVER GIVE UP!
And don’t forget, life is good in the Florida Keys; life is very good in the Florida Keys.
